note: A synagogue of the Jews of Rome opened onto a room where a corpse was lying, so the impurity of the dead spread into the synagogue, and the priests, who must avoid that impurity, could not go in to pray. They came to Rava, who told them to lift the ark and set it down in the opening between the rooms: a wooden utensil made to stay in one place cannot become impure, so it blocks the impurity. The Rabbis objected that the ark is sometimes moved with a Torah scroll still inside it, which makes it an ordinary movable utensil. Rava answered that if so, there is no remedy.
why: The Gemara is collecting Rava's rulings about the ark, its curtain and the cases that hold Torah scrolls; this case adds one more ruling of his about the ark, this time about its legal status as a wooden utensil.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage the priests consult; he proposes using the ark as a barrier, then concedes the objection.

terms.meaning: A dead body imparts the most severe form of ritual impurity, which spreads through a roofed space. Priests are forbidden to contract it.
The cabinet in a synagogue where the Torah scrolls are kept.

terms.term: a wooden utensil designated to rest
terms.meaning: In the purity laws, a large wooden object made to stay in place rather than be carried about cannot become impure, and so can act as a barrier against impurity.

note: Rav Huna once decreed a fast day. Rav Hana bar Hanilai and all the people of his town came to Rav Huna, and charity was imposed on them, which they gave. When they were about to go home, they asked Rav Huna to give the money back so they could support the poor of their own town with it. Rav Huna refused, citing a teaching that where a town has a scholar overseeing its needs, the money goes to him, and adding that the poor of his town and theirs alike rely on him.
why: A teaching just cited rules that townspeople who pledge charity while visiting another town take the money home for their own poor; this story shows the exception, when the town has a scholar in charge of its needs.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who decreed the fast and kept the charity, saying the poor of both towns rely on him.

people.name: Rav Hana bar Hanilai
people.about: He came with the people of his town to Rav Huna on the fast day.

terms.meaning: A public fast declared by the community's leaders, often in time of trouble, when people also gave charity.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.
A Torah scholar responsible for managing a community's affairs, including the use of charity funds.

note: Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Nehunya the Great what virtue had earned him a long life. Rabbi Nehunya's attendants took the question as disrespect and began beating Rabbi Akiva, who climbed to the top of a date palm. From there he asked another question: if the Torah says the daily offering is a lamb, why does it add the word one? Hearing this, Rabbi Nehunya told his attendants that he was a young Torah scholar and to let him be. He answered that one means the finest of the flock, and that his long life came because he never accepted gifts, never insisted on getting even with those who wronged him, and was openhanded with his money.
why: The Gemara is explaining each of Rabbi Nehunya's virtues by pointing to the conduct of other Sages, and goes on to similar stories of Sages asked how they merited long life.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The young scholar who asks Rabbi Nehunya about his long life and is beaten by the attendants.

people.name: Rabbi Nehunya the Great
people.about: The aged Sage who stops his attendants and answers Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: The lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and every afternoon.
